blocks.prompt: The Slowest Hunter on the Branch
blocks.text: A chameleon does not run. It rocks back and forth on a branch, slow, like a leaf in the wind. Its eyes work like two small towers. One eye can watch a bird while the other eye watches a bug. When it finds the bug, both eyes turn and look at the same spot. Then the tongue comes out. It can reach farther than the chameleon is long, and the tip is sticky. The bug is gone before it can move. People say chameleons change color to hide. That is not the real reason. A chameleon changes color to show how it feels.

blocks.prompt: The Color Is a Message
blocks.text: Almost everyone believes the same thing about chameleons: that they change color to match whatever they are sitting on. Put one on a checkered blanket, and it will turn checkered. That is not true. A chameleon cannot copy a pattern, and most of the time it is not trying to hide at all. The color is a message. A male chameleon who wants to scare off another male flares up bright yellow, orange, and red. A calm chameleon settles back into quiet green. A chameleon that has lost a fight goes dull and dark. Color is how these lizards talk, and they do most of their talking without a sound. Color also does a second job. Dark skin soaks up more heat, so a cold chameleon in the morning sun turns almost black. Once it warms up, it lightens again. The rest of the chameleon is just as odd. Its eyes swivel in two directions at once. Its feet grip like tongs. Its tail curls around a twig like a fifth hand. And its tongue can fire out farther than its whole body and snap back with a bug attached.

blocks.prompt: Not Painting. Tuning.
blocks.text: The chameleon has a reputation it does not deserve. Ask almost anyone what a chameleon does and they will tell you it blends into its background. It does not. A chameleon cannot copy a pattern, cannot turn plaid, and cannot match a wall. What it can do is stranger. For a long time people assumed the color came from pigment, the way paint mixes. It does not, at least not the bright part. Under a chameleon's outer skin lies a layer of cells packed with tiny crystals, arranged in a neat grid. Light bounces off that grid, and the spacing decides which color bounces back. When the chameleon is calm, the crystals sit close together and reflect blue. Yellow pigment sits above them, and blue plus yellow reads as green. When the chameleon gets excited, the crystals spread apart. The grid now reflects longer waves, and the animal flares yellow, orange, and red in under a minute. It is not painting itself. It is tuning itself, the way you tune a radio. So the color is not camouflage. It is speech. A male facing a rival turns loud. A defeated male turns dark and dull. A cold chameleon in the morning goes almost black to soak up heat, then pales once it is warm. Its hunting is just as precise. Each eye swivels on its own, scanning two directions at once, until a bug appears. Then both eyes lock forward together and measure the distance. The tongue does the rest. It is loaded like a bow, stretched and held, and when it releases it accelerates harder than any race car ever built, hits the bug with a sticky tip, and hauls it back. The whole strike is over before you finish blinking.

blocks.prompt: A Skin That Tunes Itself
blocks.text: Everything most people know about chameleons is wrong in an interesting way. Start with the famous trick. A chameleon does not match its background. Put one on a striped rug and you get a chameleon on a striped rug, not a striped lizard. Its color is a broadcast, not a disguise: rivals, mates, and moods. A male squaring up against another male floods with yellow and orange within seconds. The loser drains to a dull brown. A cold animal darkens at dawn to absorb sunlight, then pales as it warms. How it does this stayed a puzzle until researchers in Geneva looked closely in 2015. The bright colors are not pigment being poured in and out. Beneath the chameleon's surface sits a layer of cells called iridophores, each packed with nanocrystals of guanine arranged in a repeating lattice. Light striking that lattice reflects at a wavelength set by the spacing between crystals. Relaxed, the crystals crowd together and throw back short blue wavelengths, which combine with yellow pigment above to read as green. Excited, the crystals spread apart. The lattice widens, longer wavelengths bounce back, and green becomes yellow, orange, red. The animal is not repainting. It is retuning an optical instrument built into its own hide. A deeper second layer of larger crystals reflects near-infrared light, which is heat the chameleon does not want. The tongue is a separate piece of engineering. Muscle alone is too slow for what a chameleon needs, so it does not rely on muscle for the launch. Sheaths of collagen are wound around a bone in the throat and slowly stretched, storing energy like a drawn bow. Release it and the tongue leaves the mouth accelerating harder than any race car ever built, covering more than the animal's own body length in a fraction of a second. The tip lands with a sticky mucus roughly four hundred times thicker than your saliva, and it folds around the bug as it hits. The insect is hauled back before it registers a threat. The rest fits the same pattern of quiet extremes. The toes are fused into two opposed bundles, so each foot closes on a branch like a pair of tongs. The tail works as a fifth limb. The eyes rotate independently, giving nearly full coverage, then swing forward together to range the target. There is no ear opening and no eardrum. Around two hundred species exist, most of them in Madagascar and mainland Africa, and the smallest of them, discovered there in 2021, fits on a fingertip.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Family Chamaeleonidae, roughly 200 species
The iridophore lattice is a tunable photonic crystal

Ballistic tongue: elastic recoil, over 100 g of acceleration

blocks.prompt: How a Chameleon Really Works
blocks.text: Almost every fact people repeat about chameleons is a distortion of a more interesting fact. The famous claim is that a chameleon changes color to match its surroundings. It does not. Set one on a chessboard and it will not turn checkered. Set one against brick and it will not turn brick. A chameleon has no mechanism for copying a pattern, and much of the time it is not trying to hide at all. What it has instead is stranger, and it took biologists a long time to work out what. Color in the animal world usually comes from pigment: a molecule that absorbs some wavelengths and reflects the rest. Pigment is chemical, and chemistry is slow. A chameleon can swing from green to blazing orange in under a minute, which is far too fast for pigment to explain. In 2015, a research team in Geneva worked out what is actually happening, and the answer belongs to physics rather than chemistry. Beneath the chameleon's surface lies a layer of cells called iridophores. Each one is stacked with nanocrystals of guanine, the same compound that shows up in DNA, arranged in a regular three-dimensional lattice. A lattice like that is a photonic crystal: light hitting it reflects at a wavelength determined by the spacing between the crystals, the same way a soap bubble or a CD throws back colors it does not contain. When the chameleon is calm, the crystals sit tightly packed and the lattice returns short blue wavelengths. A layer of yellow pigment sits over the top, and blue passing through yellow reads to your eye as green. When the animal is roused, the crystals inside those cells spread apart. The lattice widens, longer wavelengths come back, and the chameleon flares yellow, then orange, then red. Nothing has been manufactured. The animal has retuned a mirror it was already wearing. There is a second iridophore layer underneath, built from larger, more disordered crystals, and it reflects near-infrared. That is not a signal at all. That is a sunshade for an animal that cannot sweat. So the color is a broadcast: status, threat, readiness, temperature. Rivals read it. Mates read it. It is language, not disguise. The tongue is the second machine, and it solves a different problem. Muscle contracts at a fixed maximum rate, and no muscle in a chameleon is fast enough to catch an alert insect. So the launch does not use muscle directly. Collagen sheaths are wound around a bone in the throat, and a muscle spends a comparatively lazy moment stretching them, loading energy into the tissue like a drawn bow. When the catch releases, that energy dumps all at once. The tongue of one small species has been measured leaving the mouth at more than a hundred times the acceleration of gravity, a load no vehicle built for a human could survive. It reaches out past twice the animal's body length, lands with mucus around four hundred times more viscous than human saliva, and the tip folds around the prey as it arrives. The elegance is in the cold. A chameleon is ectothermic, so its body temperature tracks the air, and muscle performance collapses as the air cools. Elastic recoil does not care. Stored energy releases at nearly the same speed whether the morning is warm or cold, so a chilled chameleon still fires its tongue at close to full power, even though hauling it back in, a job that does depend on muscle, becomes noticeably slower. The animal that looks slowest is running the fastest movement in its neighborhood. There are roughly two hundred chameleon species, about half of them found nowhere but Madagascar. The smallest, described there in 2021, is about the size of a sunflower seed. They are also disappearing, for reasons that have nothing to do with biology: forest clearance and the pet trade. The lizard famous for hiding turns out never to have been hiding, and now it is running out of places to be seen.
